ety.text: From Middle English sent (noun) and senten (verb), from Old French sentir (“to feel, perceive, smell, sense”), from Latin sentiō, sentīre (“to feel, sense”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”), and thus related to Saterland Frisian Sin (“sense”), West Frisian sin (“sense”), Dutch zin (“sense, meaning”), Low German Sinn (“sense”), Luxembourgish Sënn (“sense, perception”), German Sinn (“sense”). The -c- appeared in the 17th century, possibly by influence of ascent, descent, etc., or by influence of science.

senses.d: A distinctive smell.
ex: the scent of flowers / of a skunk
to give off / release / exude a scent

senses.d: A smell left by an animal that may be used for tracing.
ex: The dogs picked up / caught the scent but then quickly lost it.
He […] twice to-day pick’d out the dullest scent; / Trust me, I take him for the better dog.

senses.d: The sense of smell.
ex: I believe the bloodhound has the best scent of all dogs.
His houndes espyde him where he was, and Blacksoote first of all / And Stalker speciall good of sent began aloud to call.

senses.d: A substance (usually liquid) created to provide a pleasant smell.
ex: a scent shop

senses.d: Any trail or trace that can be followed to find something or someone, such as the paper left behind in a paperchase.
ex: The minister's off-hand remark put journalists on the scent of a cover-up.
The tip put the detectives on a false scent / the wrong scent.

senses.d: Sense, perception.

senses.d: To detect the scent of; to discern by the sense of smell.
ex: The hounds scented the fox in the woods.

senses.d: To inhale in order to detect the scent of (something).
ex: I paused to scent the breeze as I entered the valley.
One night he sprang from sleep with a start, eager-eyed, nostrils quivering and scenting,

senses.d: To have a suspicion of; to detect the possibility of (something).
ex: I scented trouble when I saw them running down the hill towards me.
Cope seemed to scent a challenge and accepted it.

senses.d: To impart an odour to, to cause to have a particular smell.
ex: Scent the air with burning sage before you begin your meditation.

senses.d: To have a smell; (figuratively) to give an impression (of something).
ex: Thunderbolts & lightnings […] do sent strongly of brimstone:

senses.d: To hunt animals by means of the sense of smell.

senses.d: The location of an event that attracts attention.
ex: the scene of the crime
Lily was pronounced dead at the scene.

senses.d: The stage.
ex: They stood in the centre of the scene.

senses.d: The decorations; furnishings, and backgrounds of a stage, representing the place in which the action of a play is set.
ex: to paint scenes
to change the scenes

senses.d: A part of a dramatic work that is set in the same place or time. In the theatre, generally a number of scenes constitute an act.
ex: The play is divided into three acts, and in total twenty-five scenes.
The most moving scene is the final one, where he realizes he has wasted his whole life.

senses.d: The location, time, circumstances, etc., in which something occurs, or in which the action of a story, play, or the like, is set up.
ex: In Troy, there lies the scene.
The world is a vast scene of strife.

senses.d: A combination of objects or events in view or happening at a given moment at a particular place.
ex: He assessed the scene to check for any danger, and agreed it was safe.
They saw an angry scene outside the pub.

senses.d: A landscape, or part of a landscape; scenery.
ex: A sylvan scene with various greens was drawn, / Shades on the sides, and in the midst a lawn.

senses.d: An exhibition of passionate or strong feeling before others, creating embarrassment or disruption; often, an artificial or affected action, or course of action, done for effect; a theatrical display.
ex: The headmistress told the students not to cause a scene.
The crazy lady made a scene in the grocery store.

senses.d: An element of fiction writing.

ex: She got into the emo scene at an early age.
